card.hook: Picture a long curve of sand, water in about five shades of turquoise, and little boats scattered toward the horizon like someone dropped them there on purpose. That's Carlisle Bay, and it's hard to take a bad photo here.
card.stand_here: Head for Pebbles Beach on the edge of the bay and stand right at the water's edge on the shoreline. Face out over the water, with the bay opening to the west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole sweep of shoreline. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull a boat on the horizon closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sea or a boat, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the water stays rich.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light is fresh and the beach is quiet. Towards sunset also works well, because the bay opens out to the west.
card.selfie_here: Try the Pebbles Beach edge early in the morning, when the light is fresh and the water shows a range of blues. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low so the bay fills the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At The Boatyard pier on Brownes Beach, ask someone to stand at the landward entrance of the pier while you walk out along it, so the open bay is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Check locally, and on the map, that the beach is open and for any shoreline or cruise-related restrictions before you go. If you snorkel, use appropriate gear and follow local guidelines.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, and keep a strip of sand in front. Then see if you can land one boat right on the horizon.
card.good_to_know: Carlisle Bay is a small natural harbour, and Bridgetown sits on its shore. It's now a marine park popular with scuba divers, and anchors and cannonballs from old ships still lie on the seabed. The bay is named after James Hay, 1st Earl of Carlisle, who claimed the island in 1627 for King Charles I.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Pebbles Beach on the edge of the bay and stand right at the water's edge on the shoreline. Face out over the water, with the bay opening to the west.

card.hook: Picture a sweep of curved stands against a bright Caribbean sky, with a ground so wide (about 360 m across) that you'll need a plan for what to squeeze in. That's Kensington Oval, and the curves do most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Head to the spot near Fontabelle and stand about 130 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the middle of the ground is 130 m away, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole sweep of the stands in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural view with seating, floodlights and sky, then try 2x-5x (if your phone has it) to pick out signs, stand names and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon on a straight line so the stands don't lean, then tap the stands and slide it a touch darker if the sky is blazing.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows than midday. Match and event days get busy around the ground, so pick a quiet day if you want clear shots.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the entrance of the Oval and stand beside the Sir Garfield Sobers statue at the gate. Several guides call the cricket-legend statues outside the ground strong photo spots, so use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and angle yourself so the statue sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Whether you can get inside depends on the event, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 2x-5x and hunt down the Three Ws stand name, then take one shot of the sign and one of the stand around it.
card.good_to_know: Cricket has been played here since 1882, when the Pickwick Cricket Club took over the ground. The first Test match was played in January 1930, West Indies against England. The stands were largely rebuilt for the 2007 Cricket World Cup, and Australia played Sri Lanka in the final here that April.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the spot near Fontabelle and stand about 130 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the middle of the ground is 130 m away, about 2 minutes on foot.

card.hook: Cruise ships are huge, and next to a long, low waterfront they look even bigger. Bridgetown Port is where Barbados says hello to its visitors, and the picture says "I've arrived" all by itself.
card.stand_here: Stand about 490 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north toward Bridgetown Port. You're some way off, so the ships and cranes will look small and neat.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole waterfront. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a ship, a crane or the quay. Use 0.5x only if you want lots of sky and water, and keep the horizon level.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the gridlines on, put the horizon on the lower or upper third line, and leave some sky and water around the ships instead of cropping tight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, kinder light than midday and less glare on the water. Which ships are in port changes the view, so check what's alongside before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Hold your phone out with the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it so the harbour and ships sit over your shoulder. Keep the horizon level and stay on public ground.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working harbour, so keep to public ground, follow any signs, and check the official site before you go because parts may be restricted. One guide describes the walk from the cruise terminal exit along the ocean up to downtown and the Careenage as safe and pleasurable.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the same ship, then see which one makes it look more gigantic.
card.good_to_know: The harbour is fairly young. Building began in 1956 and finished in 1961, and engineers made a man-made isthmus of about 90 acres to link the old shoreline off Fontabelle to little Pelican Island. Dredging in 2002 deepened the port to 11.6 metres, so some of the largest cruise ships can berth instead of anchoring offshore. It handles roughly 700,000 cruise passengers a year, so there's often something big alongside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 490 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north toward Bridgetown Port. You're some way off, so the ships and cranes will look small and neat.

selfie_research.safety: One guide describes the walk from the cruise terminal exit along the ocean up to downtown and the Careenage as safe and pleasurable.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Bridgetown port itself behind the visitor, so I am returning no selfie spots. The closest candidates were not confirmed for this purpose: Wanderlog describes 'The Stone House' as a waterfront boardwalk good for photos, but does not say where it is relative to the port. Carlisle Bay is called a popular photo spot, but no page places the port in the frame from there. Chamberlain Bridge and the Independence Arch are named as photo ops, but they are downtown, not at the port. No page gives a passer-by position for photographing a visitor with the whole port in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, so rules is empty. The coordinates 13.106, -59.632 fall close to the cruise terminal area; a MarineTraffic photo taken at 13.102, -59.632 is captioned with cruise vessels, which supports that identification. Sources: Wanderlog 'The 18 best photo spots in Bridgetown'; iqcruising Barbados cruise port guide; cruiseports.ca Barbados page; MarineTraffic photo 3909201.

card.hook: Picture a wide green oval, a racecourse wrapped around it, and a Georgian guardhouse with a domed clock tower standing guard at the edge. Guides call it the most photographed building in the Garrison, so make it your first shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Main Guard House & Clock Tower, right at the front of the building, and face the grass. The savannah itself is about 250 m to the east, stretching away behind your shot.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the guardhouse and clock tower, so the building keeps its natural shape. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you want the colonnade, the tower and the open grass all in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the clock tower, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the pale stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows under the arches. If you're here on a Thursday, there's a ceremony at noon, and a short Live Photo can catch the movement.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the old cannons in front of the Main Guard and clock tower. Use the front camera and tip it so the savannah and the historic buildings sit behind your shoulder. Check the frame on screen first, because the exact angle depends on where you stand. For something different, Pebbles Beach next to the Garrison is a popular early-morning spot while racehorses bathe in the sea, but the Garrison won't be behind you there.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the open ground in front of the Main Guard with the building behind you, and ask a passer-by to take the photo from out on the grass.
card.rules_and_safety: The track is ticketed on race days, so check the official site before you go. There's little shade on the savannah, so bring a refillable water bottle.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and put the clock tower dome on one of them, with the horizon dead level and not one wonky column. Bonus points if the sky is still blue.
card.good_to_know: Racing has gone on here since a British garrison was stationed on the spot. The Barbados Gold Cup is held here every year, along with the Barbados Triple Crown series for Thoroughbreds. In 2012, a network of tunnels was found under the area.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Main Guard House & Clock Tower, right at the front of the building, and face the grass. The savannah itself is about 250 m to the east, stretching away behind your shot.

card.hook: This museum used to be a Military Prison, and the thick old walls still look like it. Funnily enough, that makes it a great backdrop for a relaxed photo.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon, which sits in the middle of the Barbados Museum outline at the historic Garrison. Then walk out towards the edge of the outline, or to one side, and turn back to face the building until the walls and roofline fit.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for natural-looking walls and rooflines. If you're close and can't fit the building in, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or 5x for close-ups of stonework, doorways or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges with them so the walls don't lean, then tap the building and slide to darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the old stonework than midday sun. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the open ground of the Garrison Savannah beside the museum, with the museum building behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if you want more of the building in, and keep it over your shoulder. The exact standing point isn't pinned down, so step back until the walls fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Some galleries inside restrict photography, so ask at the entrance and check for 'no photo' signs before you shoot indoors. Check the official site for visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the walls stand perfectly straight on the gridlines and nobody wanders through the frame. Harder than it sounds!
card.good_to_know: The museum began here in 1933, in a building that was made for a very different purpose. Its collections run to more than 500,000 items, including antique maps and paintings. In 1993 it also took on the Newton Slave Burial Ground site in Christ Church.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon, which sits in the middle of the Barbados Museum outline at the historic Garrison. Then walk out towards the edge of the outline, or to one side, and turn back to face the building until the walls and roofline fit.

card.hook: Picture a 19-year-old George Washington stepping off a boat in the tropics in 1751, years before he was anyone's president. This ochre house on Bush Hill is where he stayed.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, then stand outside on the lawn in front of George Washington House on Bush Hill. Face the house and step back until the whole building fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole house. If you're close and can't fit it all in, try 0.5x. Then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the plaque and any details you like.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the walls and roofline straight, and if the sky is bright, tap the house and slide the brightness down a touch so the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls. Midday shadows can be harsh.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the lawn out front with the house behind you, so the ochre facade fills the background. Use your front camera and hold it a little low and at arm's length so the roofline sneaks in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn and shoot toward the house, so the whole facade and roofline fit, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the house, but without flash, because flash can damage the artifacts. It's a museum, so check the official site before you go, as visiting arrangements can vary.
card.challenge: Grab a matched pair: one straight, gridline-perfect wide shot of the whole house, and one close-up of the 1997 plaque.
card.good_to_know: Washington came here in 1751 with his half-brother Lawrence, who hoped the tropics would help his health. Barbados is the only place outside the United States he ever visited. The house opened as a museum in January 2007.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, then stand outside on the lawn in front of George Washington House on Bush Hill. Face the house and step back until the whole building fits in your frame.

card.hook: Here's a bridge that does a party trick: the whole span tips up to let boats slip through. Catch it mid-lift and your photo of an ordinary harbour turns into something much more fun.
card.stand_here: From the Careenage waterfront near National Heroes Square, the bridge is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. Stand in Independence Square Park at the bridge's southern end, then turn to look back across the bridge and the water towards the Parliament Buildings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the bridge and the water. Go 0.5x to squeeze the arch, the bridge and the boats into one shot, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Parliament Buildings or a single boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and set the bridge along a lower line, then tap the bridge and slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Light and boat traffic change quickly here, so take a few frames from each end of the bridge. If you're lucky the span will lift for a boat, so give it a minute or two.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden boardwalk just west of the bridge: use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the bridge over your shoulder. The Independence Arch at the Independence Square end also works if you want it behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from near the Waterfront Café, where the bridge's arches show up best, with you posed so the bridge sits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is pedestrian-only and lifts for boats, so access can change briefly. Check the official site before you go for any closures.
card.challenge: Get a shot with a boat sliding past the raised span, then another from the middle of the bridge looking along the moored yachts. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The current bridge opened in 2006 and is made from lightweight fibre-reinforced plastic. It replaced a steel swing bridge from 1872, named after Joseph Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary who helped fund repairs after the 1898 hurricane. The arch at the southern end was added in 1987 to mark 21 years of Barbados Independence.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: From the Careenage waterfront near National Heroes Square, the bridge is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. Stand in Independence Square Park at the bridge's southern end, then turn to look back across the bridge and the water towards the Parliament Buildings.

card.hook: Pop quiz: where's Lord Nelson? He used to stand at the western end of this square, but he moved out in 2020, so don't go hunting for him. What's left is a big, open slice of everyday Bridgetown, and it makes a great scene-setter.
card.stand_here: Stand near Wharf Road, about 25 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole width of the square in. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines so the horizon stays level, and keep a little of the buildings in the frame so it says 'central Bridgetown' and not just 'empty space'.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows. Midday sun can be harsh on an open square.
card.selfie_here: Try Chamberlain Bridge over the Careenage, with the colourful boats in front of you and the square behind. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in, and check the framing on site to make sure the square really is over your shoulder. The landscaped Fountain Garden by the Dolphin Fountain is another good spot, but you'll need to pick your own angle there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the southern edge of the square beside the Careenage, facing north, while you stand in front of them with the Cenotaph beyond you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed throughout the square and the museum, and personal photography generally has no restrictions. Professional or commercial shoots might need permits, and there's no flash inside the Parliament chambers.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd, then catch one lone person strolling across the square so your photo has a little scale and a story.
card.good_to_know: The square used to be called Trafalgar Square. It became National Heroes Square on 22 April 1999 (effective 28 April 1999), a name that honours the Barbadian National Heroes. The Nelson statue was unveiled in 1813, and distances from Bridgetown were traditionally measured from its base. It's now at the Barbados Museum, so older photos will look different.

card.hook: Picture a row of bobbing fishing boats, a calm strip of water, and a Gothic clock tower standing behind them like it planned the whole thing. That's the postcard shot of Bridgetown.
card.stand_here: Stand on Chamberlain Bridge, beside the Careenage inlet. Face north and the Parliament clock tower and buildings sit across the water, framed by the moored fishing boats.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the boats, water and Parliament façade in one go. Want a lot of boats up front? Try zoom 0.5x, but keep the tower away from the edge so it doesn't lean. Zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) picks out the clock tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the tower on a vertical line and let the water and boats fill the bottom third.
card.best_time: The best morning light can vary, so check on the day. Try a morning visit and a later-in-the-day visit if you can. The bridge can get crowded, so give yourself time to wait for a gap.
card.selfie_here: Do it on Chamberlain Bridge, on the bridge deck over the Careenage. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and turn so the Parliament Buildings sit across the water behind your shoulder. It's a busy photo stop, so take a few tries.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in National Heroes Square, the open plaza in front of Parliament, to walk around until they find an angle that fits the whole building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to exterior shots. Photography in the chambers is restricted and flash isn't allowed in there. The interior is open only for tours and the museum, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead upright with a boat in the foreground, then check the gridlines to see if you nailed it.
card.good_to_know: The Parliament Buildings are a pair of neo-Gothic buildings built between 1870 and 1874. Parliament has met here since 16 June 1874. In 2011 both were designated as protected properties within the World Heritage Site of Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Chamberlain Bridge, beside the Careenage inlet. Face north and the Parliament clock tower and buildings sit across the water, framed by the moored fishing boats.

card.hook: Forget the single big monument on Broad Street. The star here is the whole street, with buildings on both sides and the road running off into the distance.
card.stand_here: Stand on Lower Broad Street, about 160 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a first wide shot from there, then stroll towards the street and keep snapping as the view opens up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural-looking street scene. Switch to 0.5x if the pavement is narrow or you want a whole row of buildings in one go. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details, or to squeeze the view along the street.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up along one of them so it leads the eye into the picture, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Softer light earlier or later in the day is usually kinder to street scenes than harsh midday sun. Pick a time that suits you and check the result on your screen.
card.selfie_here: Head into National Heroes Square, which sits on Broad Street, directly across from the Parliament Buildings. Use the front camera (or 0.5x) and put the Parliament Buildings over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of Broad St and Rickett St, by the West Wing of the Parliament Buildings, and frame you with the building behind you (check this corner on the map first).
card.rules_and_safety: Step to the edge of the pavement before you stop for a photo, and keep an eye on traffic and people while you frame. Photos are allowed throughout the square, but flash is not allowed inside the chambers.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap, then catch one passer-by walking into your street shot so the scene gets a bit of life and scale.
card.good_to_know: Broad Street is a public street in Bridgetown. It works best when you can see its length, so aim to show the buildings on both sides rather than one monument. Check local conditions and the official tourism information for Bridgetown before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Lower Broad Street, about 160 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a first wide shot from there, then stroll towards the street and keep snapping as the view opens up.

card.hook: You could walk right past this one. The only synagogue in Barbados hides behind a plain wrought-iron gate on a quiet lane in the middle of Bridgetown, and that gate is the best prop you'll get.
card.stand_here: Stand on Synagogue Lane, right in front of the wrought-iron entrance gate. Face the gate square-on, with the main synagogue site to the north-west of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the gate and buildings keep a natural shape. If the lane is too tight to fit the frontage, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep your phone level so the gate doesn't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the gateposts upright, then tap the building behind the bars so they don't steal the sharpness.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the shade is less harsh. The lane is likely quieter outside the middle of the day. If the sky is bright and the walls look washed out, drag the slider to make the picture a little darker.
card.selfie_here: Inside the gate, the cobblestone courtyard is named as a photo area, and so is the landscaped gazebo path in the grounds. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and check on the spot whether the synagogue fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Inside, stand in the graveyard among the old headstones and ask a passer-by to shoot back toward the synagogue building.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography without flash is allowed in the museum and courtyard, but not during Shabbat or holiday services. Check for restrictions inside the sanctuary itself. The courtyard, cemetery and synagogue are behind a gated, ticketed entrance, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get both gateposts perfectly straight, with the bars framing the buildings like a picture frame and not one blurry bar in sight?
card.good_to_know: The first building here dates from 1654. A hurricane destroyed it in 1831 and it was rebuilt. In 2008 a mikveh, a ritual bath probably from the 17th century, was found on the grounds, and in 2011 the synagogue and the mikveh were designated UNESCO protected properties within Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Synagogue Lane, right in front of the wrought-iron entrance gate. Face the gate square-on, with the main synagogue site to the north-west of you.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: a UNESCO World Heritage fort is tucked inside the grounds of a beach resort, and its cannons still point out to sea like they're on duty.
card.stand_here: Stand at the bastion on the tip of Needham's Point, where Charles Fort's best-preserved stonework sits. The phone icon on the map is right at the fort, so there's no extra walk. Face out towards Carlisle Bay with the cannons in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the bastion, the cannons and the bay in one shot. Go to 0.5x for more of the battlements and the sweep of the bay, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single cannon or ships on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide the picture a little darker so the sky and sea keep their colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour is lovely, or go early morning for softer light and fewer people.
card.selfie_here: Climb up to the ramparts, the battlements facing out over Carlisle Bay, and use the front camera at 0.5x so the old stonework and the bay fit in behind you.
card.ask_someone: If you spot someone on the beach by the Hilton, ask them to shoot the fort from the sand, which is a view the fort is often photographed from.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort sits on grounds leased by the Hilton Barbados Resort, so access may depend on the hotel or on guided tours. Check locally before you go. There's little signage and some cannons are missing, so look around the bastion before choosing your angle.
card.challenge: Take one shot standing and one crouching beside the same cannon, then see which gives the cleaner line against the water.
card.good_to_know: The fort began as Needham's Fort in 1650 to protect the bay and Bridgetown. It was renamed Charles Fort in 1660 when Charles II returned to the throne, and rebuilt in 1811. George Washington visited in 1751-1752 and dined with the Captain here more than once.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the bastion on the tip of Needham's Point, where Charles Fort's best-preserved stonework sits. The phone icon on the map is right at the fort, so there's no extra walk. Face out towards Carlisle Bay with the cannons in front of you.

card.hook: On a calm day the Careenage gives you everything twice: once for real, and once upside down in the water. Bridgetown's waterfront hands you foreground, middle distance and sky without any hunting.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in Independence Square, about 290 m east of the subject, and face west. Then stroll towards the water for closer shots with something in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view. If the scene is wider than your screen, go to 0.5x and keep the horizon level. For a single boat, a reflection or a detail on the far bank, try 2x up to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and include a boat, mooring or railing close to you for depth.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections. Looking west, the sun will be in front of you late in the day, so check the screen for glare. Tap the screen on the part you care about and slide it a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.selfie_here: Try the Chamberlain Bridge near the Parliament Buildings, where reviewers say the views over the Careenage are the nicest. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and keep the water and boats over your shoulder. The Charles Duncan O'Neal Bridge is another classic inlet view, best in soft morning or late afternoon light.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Chamberlain Bridge facing west, while you stand in front of them with the Careenage and the boats behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access and any local rules along the waterfront aren't confirmed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a boat's reflection and frame it with a railing or mooring in the foreground, then take three shots as the water shifts.
card.good_to_know: The Careenage is a stretch of waterfront right in the middle of Bridgetown. Boats and people move, and the water changes the reflections from one moment to the next, so take a few frames. No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check local options for getting to central Bridgetown.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon in Independence Square, about 290 m east of the subject, and face west. Then stroll towards the water for closer shots with something in the foreground.

card.hook: The trees around St. Michael's Cathedral have strong opinions about where you can take your photo, and they win most arguments. Don't fight them. Treat the cathedral like a walk-around and let the branches be part of the picture.
card.stand_here: Start on St Michael Row, two blocks east of National Heroes Square, and face the cathedral's coral-stone front. Then stroll around the outside, stopping often, until you find a clear line between the trees.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x to fit the whole building in. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you're close and the trees leave you no room. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the tower or stonework between branches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, then tap the stonework and slide darker a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the walls.
card.best_time: There's no single perfect hour here, so pick a time when you can wander round without rushing. Services are held on Sundays and Wednesdays, when things may be busier and quiet matters, so give those a miss for photos.
card.selfie_here: The churchyard gardens on St. Michael's Row are the pick, among the old headstones and big shady trees. Use the front camera (try the wider option if your phone has one) and keep the church behind you, but remember the gates may be locked.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working church with regular services, so be patient and quiet if people are coming and going. The churchyard gates may be locked, so don't count on getting in. Scaffolding or covered areas may show up in your shots while restoration fundraising continues.
card.challenge: Take one photo of the tower peeking through the branches, then try to find a second frame where a tree is your picture frame instead of your problem.
card.good_to_know: St. Michael's is the tallest Anglican place of worship in Barbados. It was first consecrated in 1665, rebuilt in 1789 after a hurricane, and made a cathedral in 1825. The churchyard holds the graves of Grantley Adams and his son Tom Adams, both major figures in Barbadian politics.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on St Michael Row, two blocks east of National Heroes Square, and face the cathedral's coral-stone front. Then stroll around the outside, stopping often, until you find a clear line between the trees.

card.hook: Picture a proper Georgian house sitting on open lawns, with a tree nearby that's said to be almost 1,000 years old. Queen's Park gives you both, and you don't even have to walk far.
card.stand_here: Stand at Queen's Park House, on the lawn right in front of it. Face back toward the park lawns so the house, the grass and lots of sky all fit in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole house and lawns. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the front of the house. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for windows, the bandstand or the baobab bark.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up the house so its walls look straight, and put it a little off-centre with lawn in the foreground.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. The light is softer on the front of the house and the shade under the trees is less harsh.
card.selfie_here: Head to the giant baobab in the playground area east of Queen's Park House and stand beside it with the front camera. The trunk shows off how huge it is. For a second one, stand at the bandstand with its ironwork rising behind you, and try 0.5x if your front camera has it.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is public, but the house, theatre and gallery may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go. The park may be refurbished or renamed, so check current access too.
card.challenge: Fill your whole screen with baobab trunk, then step back and see how small a friend looks next to it.
card.good_to_know: The first Queen's Park House was destroyed in the great hurricane of 1780, and the house was rebuilt in the 1780s. It was the home of the commander of the British troops in Barbados. Today it holds the Daphne Joseph Hackett theatre and the Queen's Park Gallery, and the park opened to the public on 10 June 1909. The baobab is one of only two on the island and is about 18 m around the trunk.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Queen's Park House, on the lawn right in front of it. Face back toward the park lawns so the house, the grass and lots of sky all fit in.

card.hook: You'll spot a small white tower with a black lantern for a hat, and then you'll realise the big hotel is doing its best to hide it. Good news: the beach has the view.
card.stand_here: Head to the beach just south of the Hilton, at the phone icon on the map, and face the tower. It's the only place you can see it, because the hotel's block of rooms hides it from everywhere else.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the tower with the sea behind it. Then try zoom 2x to bring it closer and keep the hotel buildings out of your picture.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white tower, then make the picture a touch darker so the white paint keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the white paint. The hotel grounds are often quieter then too.
card.selfie_here: Try Needham's Point beach at the southern end of Carlisle Bay, on the sand near the pier that juts out into the harbour. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x, and keep the lighthouse over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to face the tower and take the shot while you stand in front of it, so you and the white tower fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The lane in is very narrow, so go slowly and allow extra time. The tower is closed to visitors and sits on private hotel grounds, so ask at the hotel if you're unsure about access.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands tall and straight, then see if you can keep it in the middle third with lots of sea and sky around it.
card.good_to_know: The lighthouse dates from 1855 and is one of four historic lighthouses still standing on Barbados. It had a steady light instead of a rotating one, and its lens was half red and half green so sailors could tell which side of the bay they were on. It no longer works as a lighthouse, and the Hilton, which owns it, has partly restored it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the beach just south of the Hilton, at the phone icon on the map, and face the tower. It's the only place you can see it, because the hotel's block of rooms hides it from everywhere else.

card.hook: Forget the grand sweeping view. This one is all about a shack front, a name on the wall and a bit of local colour. Keep it simple and let the little details tell your story.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon near Aquatic Gap. The shack is 3 m from it, to the south-east, so just a few steps that way. Face south-east and you're looking right at the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the shack front. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front in, then zoom 2x for tighter shots of the signage or small details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the shack's edges with them, so the walls look straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Daylight is best, so you can see the shack and its details clearly. If midday light is harsh, try earlier or later.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if there's room, and keep the shack's sign over your shoulder. Hold your phone level so the walls stay straight behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place, so keep out of the way of customers and staff, and ask before photographing people up close. Check locally whether it's open and whether you can stop there comfortably.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one of the whole shack front, and one close-up of a single detail that catches your eye.
card.good_to_know: Cuzz's Fish Shack is a small, casual food spot in Bridgetown, Barbados. It's a working business rather than a sight, so check locally or ask on the spot before you go. No public transport stops are listed nearby, so check a local map for how to get there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon near Aquatic Gap. The shack is 3 m from it, to the south-east, so just a few steps that way. Face south-east and you're looking right at the front.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot or a photo-taking position for Cuzz's Fish Shack. The only location details are about where the stand sits: a beach parking lot immediately south of the Radisson Aquatica entrance at Pebbles Beach (Uncommon Caribbean), and Pebbles Beach generally (Caribjournal, Wanderlog). Tripadvisor photo captions mention 'the stand in the car park', but those are food photos, not landmark-behind-you spots, so I did not list them. Location sources disagree: VisitBarbados says between Hilton and Radisson Aquatica in Hastings, Christ Church; Facebook says Hastings on Carlisle Bay; YourBajanGuide says Brown's Beach near Barbados Blue Watersports; RestaurantSnapshot says Needham's Point. The coordinates you gave match the Pebbles Beach listing (SavorEverything), so Pebbles Beach is the best map anchor. Opening hours also vary: Caribjournal gives Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and a Tripadvisor reviewer says it opens at 10 a.m., not 8 a.m. as stated online. Verify the spot on the ground before adding it to the app.
